question: What training-dynamics transition underlies language-model loss scaling, and can per-token gradient interference explain why larger models improve both before and after that transition?

key_findings.claim: Language-model loss curves exhibit an early smoothly broken power law: larger models reach a lower loss at the break and improve faster afterward.
key_findings.evidence: One-break BNSL fits over models from 14M to 472M parameters plus OLMo checkpoints reproduce final loss within roughly 1% and yield break loss, break step, and post-break rate summaries.

key_findings.claim: The paper defines zero-sum learning as cancellation among per-token loss changes and observes that its destructive-interference statistic rises sharply around deceleration.
key_findings.evidence: The factorization |delta L| = mean(|delta ell|) times one minus destructive interference separates shrinking token-level changes from cancellation; the reported cancellation change explains about a tenfold slowdown versus 1.5-fold from magnitude shrinkage.

key_findings.claim: Per-token gradient opposition is linked to loss-change cancellation using a first-order projection, and the approximation correlates strongly with observed token losses after deceleration.
key_findings.evidence: One-dimensional checkpoint-to-update loss slices and a 1,000-token sample support local linearity; progressive sharpening is rejected because measured directional sharpness falls rather than rises near the break.

key_findings.claim: The account of scale is incomplete: early gains are attributed mainly to larger gradient norms, while post-break gains are inferred from a larger number of coordinates with lower interference even though average coordinate interference worsens.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly leave direct scale-independent mitigation open and note that single-step gradients do not reconcile the multi-step interactions used in key loss-change measurements.

method.core_idea: Fit a break in loss trajectories, then decompose aggregate loss progress into per-token magnitude and cancellation terms and connect cancellation to gradient geometry.
method.mechanism: BNSL identifies the transition; per-token loss deltas, proxy gradients, update-direction slices, and scale sweeps test whether destructive opposition grows and whether larger parameter spaces retain more shared directions.
assumptions: A one-break BNSL identifies a meaningful qualitative transition rather than a flexible curve-fit artifact.
Per-token measurements and gradient proxies represent the full training distribution.
First-order single-update geometry explains the multi-step loss changes used to quantify zero-sum learning.

techniques.role: Extracts loss and time at deceleration plus the post-break log-log rate.
Separates mean loss-change magnitude from destructive cancellation.
Tests first-order assumptions and alternative sharpness explanations around checkpoints.

evaluations.setting: Transformer language models from 14M to 472M parameters on C4, with OLMo-1B/7B reference curves and optimizer/data ablations.
evaluations.metric: BNSL fit error and break parameters.
evaluations.result: A consistent early deceleration is fit, and size lowers break loss and improves the post-break rate.
evaluations.baseline: Single power-law interpretation and alternative training configurations.

evaluations.setting: Per-token losses, proxy gradients and update-direction landscapes across training.
evaluations.metric: Destructive-interference statistics, first-order correlation, gradient norms and directional sharpness.
evaluations.result: Cancellation rises near deceleration and dominates the measured slowdown; local linearity strengthens after the break.
evaluations.baseline: Token-change magnitude reduction and progressive sharpening as alternative explanations.

limitations: The evidence is restricted to cross-entropy scaling with model size on web-text transformers.
The BNSL fit detects correlation and does not itself prove a phase transition.
Gradient analysis is primarily single-step while major loss-delta measurements span many steps.
The suggested scale-independent intervention is not designed or tested.
failure_modes: A schedule change or data-mixture transition can create an apparent curve break unrelated to the proposed mechanism.
Coordinate-wise gradient opposition is parameterization dependent.
Token sampling and gradient proxies can overstate cancellation or miss rare shared directions.
reusable_insights: Aggregate training curves can hide cancellation between examples even when individual examples remain learnable.
A mechanistic scaling account should decompose both where a trajectory changes and how scale alters each term.
Alternative mechanisms such as sharpening should be measured on the same checkpoints rather than dismissed conceptually.
open_questions: Can an optimizer reduce post-break cancellation and improve held-out loss at fixed model size and compute?
Does loss deceleration occur in vision, multimodal, or reinforcement-learning scaling?
Which conclusions survive function-space or representation-invariant gradient measures?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaplan et al. predict loss from resources; the target seeks a within-training mechanism and a break-point decomposition behind model-size gains.

competitive_landscape.title: Broken Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct functional-form predecessor used to measure deceleration.
competitive_landscape.difference: Caballero et al. introduce the flexible broken-power-law family across domains; the target applies a one-break form to training time and assigns the break a gradient-interference mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Competing mechanistic theory based on variance, resolution and data geometry.
competitive_landscape.difference: Bahri et al. explain data/model scaling regimes through limits and manifold/kernel resolution; the target instead analyzes finite-time per-token optimization interference in transformers.

novelty_assessment: The distinctive claim is that a measurable within-run loss break is dominated by per-token cancellation and systematically mitigated by model dimension. Broken power laws and geometric scaling theories already exist, and the proposed causal mechanism remains partly proxy-based and not interventionally validated.
reviewer_notes: Read all 35 extracted pages, including BNSL sensitivity, token-gradient proxies, multi-step contradictions, architecture/optimizer ablations, and cosine-decay replication. Primary competitor pages were checked on 2026-08-23.
